    How it works

    Each line is read for an amount, a unit and the ingredient. The amount is multiplied, then written back in the unit you'd actually reach for: 12 teaspoons becomes ¼ cup, and half of ¼ cup becomes 2 tablespoons. Fractions are rounded to the nearest ⅛, and anything that wouldn't round cleanly stays in spoons, so nothing is quietly off by more than a few percent. Lines without an amount, like "pinch of salt", are left alone.

    It understands fractions (1 1/2, 1½, ¾), ranges (2–3 cups), abbreviations (c, tbsp, T, tsp, t, oz, g, ml) and weights in brackets like "1 cup (120 g) flour". Everything happens in your browser; the recipe isn't sent anywhere.

    What doesn't scale in a straight line

    Ingredients scale cleanly; cooking doesn't always. A doubled cake batter needs a bigger pan or two pans, and a deeper pan bakes longer. Eggs don't split well, so round to whole eggs or beat one and use part of it. Salt and strong spices are safest scaled a little under and adjusted to taste. Baking soda and baking powder scale fine for doubling, but for very large batches many bakers cut back slightly.

    Questions

    How do I scale a recipe by servings?

    Enter how many the recipe makes and how many you need. The scaler divides one by the other, so a recipe for 12 scaled to 30 is multiplied by 2.5.

    How do I halve ⅓ cup?

    Half of ⅓ cup is 2⅔ tablespoons, which is 2 tablespoons plus 2 teaspoons. The scaler switches to spoons automatically, because ⅙ cup isn’t on any measuring set.

    What do I do with half an egg?

    Beat the egg, then use about half by weight or volume: a large egg is roughly 50 g or 3 tablespoons, so half is about 25 g or 1½ tablespoons.

    Does it change baking time?

    No. Time and pan size depend on how deep the batter is, not just how much there is. If you double a recipe, use a second pan of the same size and the original time will be close.
